questions.stem: The relationship between AI and ML is:
options: All AI is ML, since every AI system learns from the data it is given
ML is the broader field; AI is the subset concerned with human-like reasoning
All ML is AI, but not all AI is ML
They overlap substantially, but neither contains the other
questions.explanation: AI is the broad field of systems simulating human intelligence; ML is the subset that learns from data rather than following explicitly programmed rules. A hand-coded rule-based expert system is AI but not ML — that single example disposes of (A), (B) and (D).

questions.stem: The DevOps cycle consists of:
options: 6 stages — Plan, Develop, Build, Test, Deploy, Monitor
8 stages — Plan, Develop, Build, Test, Release, Deploy, Operate, Monitor
8 stages — Plan, Code, Build, Test, Release, Deploy, Operate, Secure
7 stages — Plan, Develop, Build, Test, Release, Deploy, Monitor
questions.explanation: 8 — Note that (C) also has eight stages, so counting alone does not get you there — the stage names matter. Automating the middle of this cycle is CI/CD.

questions.stem: The five goals of DevOps are:
options: Speed, scalability, security, collaboration, and monitoring and feedback
Speed, automation, CI/CD, collaboration, and monitoring and feedback
Plan, develop, build, test and release
Automation, version control, testing, deployment and documentation
questions.explanation: (A) alters two words and reads perfectly plausibly — scalability and security are things DevOps supports, not goals in the syllabus list. The central idea is that development and operations work as one team rather than throwing releases over a wall.

questions.stem: CI/CD stands for:
options: Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment
Continuous Improvement / Continuous Delivery
Continuous Inspection / Continuous Debugging
Code Integration / Code Distribution
questions.explanation: It is an automated pipeline that builds, tests and deploys on every code submission, so defects surface within minutes rather than at a quarterly release. (B) is the sharpest trap — Continuous Delivery is a real term in this space, but it does not pair with "Continuous Improvement".

questions.stem: RPA is best described as:
options: A platform that coordinates an end-to-end workflow across several departments
A model that learns the steps of a task by observing a human perform it repeatedly
Software bots that automate repetitive, rule-based tasks a human would otherwise perform on a computer
Physical robots performing repetitive operations on a production line
questions.explanation: RPA clicks buttons, enters data, copies and pastes, reads emails and files. It works with existing software, involves no physical robots, and crucially does not learn — which is what makes (B) wrong. (A) is BPA.

questions.stem: BPA differs from RPA because BPA:
options: Operates on physical equipment, whereas RPA operates only on software
Automates a single repetitive task, whereas RPA coordinates the whole workflow
Uses machine learning to adapt, whereas RPA follows fixed rules
Automates an entire business process, typically spanning multiple departments and systems
questions.explanation: RPA automates a task; BPA automates a process. (B) is that distinction stated backwards. Examples of BPA: employee onboarding, customer onboarding with background checks, IT service desk support, marketing automation.

questions.stem: Which automates the process of building, testing and shipping software itself, rather than a business task?
options: DevOps
BPA
RPA
Shell scripting
questions.explanation: DevOps — RPA automates a human's computer task and BPA a cross-department workflow. (D) is the honest near-miss: shell scripting is a tool used to automate build steps, but DevOps is the named practice and culture that the syllabus is asking about.

questions.stem: MLOps exists primarily because:
options: Machine learning code is usually written in different languages from the rest of the application
Machine learning models are too large to move through a standard CI/CD pipeline
Neural network weights cannot be stored in a version control system
Models degrade as the data they encounter changes over time, and manual retraining and redeployment is slow and error-prone
questions.explanation: MLOps adds monitoring of model performance and data drift, versioning of data, weights and training configurations (DVC, MLflow), and ML pipelines (Airflow, Kubeflow). The other options describe inconveniences, not the reason the discipline exists.

questions.stem: The three stages of MLOps are:
options: Design → Training → Deployment
Design → Model Development → Operations
Collect → Train → Monitor
Plan → Model Development → Operations
questions.explanation: Each distractor changes one term, and (D) changes only the first word. MLOps is not an explicit NESA dot point, so use it as evidence of depth when discussing how an ML solution is developed and maintained.

questions.stem: Data drift means:
options: The training set's distribution differs from the test set's at the time of training
The training dataset was corrupted or partially lost during storage
The model's predictions become slower as the dataset it queries grows
The data a deployed model encounters changes over time, degrading its accuracy
questions.explanation: (A) is the finest distinction here: that is train–test skew, a training-time sampling problem, whereas drift happens after deployment as the world itself changes. Drift is why a deployed model is an ongoing operational commitment requiring monitoring and scheduled retraining, not a finished artefact.

questions.stem: MLOps versions which additional artefacts that DevOps typically does not?
options: Container images and deployment manifests
Source code, configuration files and infrastructure definitions
Data, model weights and training configurations
Test suites and their expected outputs
questions.explanation: (A), (B) and (D) are all things a mature DevOps pipeline already versions — the question asks what MLOps adds. Without versioned data and weights a model result cannot be reproduced, which is the ML equivalent of losing the source code.

questions.stem: Supervised learning is characterised by:
options: Labelled data — both the input and the correct output are supplied during training
Unlabelled data, from which the model infers its own groupings
A reward signal returned by an environment after each action taken
A small labelled set used to generate labels for a much larger unlabelled set
questions.explanation: Classification and regression are the two supervised problem types. The distractors are, in order, unsupervised, reinforcement and semi-supervised learning — all four training types appear as options, so this must be answered on the definition.

questions.stem: Grouping customers by purchasing behaviour with no predefined categories is:
options: Supervised learning
Unsupervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Semi-supervised learning
questions.explanation: Unsupervised — the model finds patterns or groupings on its own, with no correct answer supplied. Algorithms include K-Means and DBSCAN. The phrase "no predefined categories" is the tell.

questions.stem: Semi-supervised learning uses:
options: Unlabelled data only, with a human confirming the resulting groupings afterwards
Labelled data only, but with the labels revealed progressively during training
A small quantity of labelled data together with a large quantity of unlabelled data
A reward signal supplemented by occasional labelled examples
questions.explanation: (A) is the sharpest trap — a human checking clusters after the fact is still unsupervised learning, because no label influenced the training. Semi-supervised learning captures much of supervised learning's accuracy without the cost of labelling everything, and labelling is often the most expensive part of an ML project.

questions.stem: Reinforcement learning trains a model by:
options: Grouping unlabelled records and refining those groups over successive passes
Supplying the correct output for every training example and correcting its errors
Having it interact with an environment and adjust its behaviour to maximise reward over time
Fine-tuning an already-trained model on a smaller, task-specific dataset
questions.explanation: Used in game playing, robotics and dynamic control — problems where the right action is revealed only through its consequences. (D) is transfer learning, a real technique that is not one of the four training types.

questions.stem: The exploration versus exploitation trade-off means balancing:
options: Spending compute on training the model against spending it on serving predictions
Trying new actions to discover better strategies against using known good strategies to maximise reward
Fitting the training data closely against generalising well to unseen data
Favouring precision against favouring recall in a classifier
questions.explanation: Pure exploitation locks in a mediocre strategy; pure exploration never cashes in. (C) is the overfitting/underfitting trade-off and (D) is the precision–recall trade-off — three genuine trade-offs from the same module, only one of which belongs to RL.

questions.stem: Which analytics type answers "What should we do?"
options: Prescriptive
Diagnostic
Predictive
Descriptive
questions.explanation: Prescriptive — e.g. recommending a marketing strategy. Descriptive summarises what happened, diagnostic explains why it happened, predictive forecasts what will happen. The four form a ladder, and the verb in the question tells you which rung.

questions.stem: Data wrangling includes all of the following except:
options: Filling missing values with the mean, or removing the affected records
Converting categorical text into numbers, e.g. "Yes" → 1
Scaling numerical values so that features with large ranges do not dominate
Choosing how many hidden layers the network will contain
questions.explanation: that is a model architecture decision, not data preparation. Wrangling also covers removing duplicates and correcting errors. The test: does the step change the data, or the model?

questions.stem: Scaling numerical features before training matters because:
options: It converts categorical text values into a numeric form the model can process
Features on very different scales, such as salary and age, would otherwise dominate distance and weight calculations
It reduces the size of the dataset, so training completes more quickly
It removes outliers, which would otherwise distort the model's predictions
questions.explanation: It is particularly critical for distance-based algorithms such as KNN, where an unscaled salary column measured in tens of thousands would swamp an age column measured in tens. (D) is the tempting one: scaling compresses the effect of outliers but does not remove them.

questions.stem: NLP underpins which applications?
options: Virtual personal assistants and chatbots
Image recognition and object detection
Route optimisation and logistics scheduling
Predictive maintenance from equipment sensor readings
questions.explanation: Its named challenges are accents and dialects, and context understanding across a multi-turn conversation. The other three are all real ML application areas — they simply are not language problems.

questions.stem: In image recognition, a multi-layered network typically detects features in which order?
options: Colours → textures → text labels
Whole objects → simple shapes → edges
Edges → simple shapes → whole objects
Pixels → weights → labels
questions.explanation: Early layers detect the simplest possible features and each subsequent layer composes those into something larger — (B) is that hierarchy inverted. Accuracy depends on the quantity and variety of training data, and the usual architecture is a CNN.

questions.stem: A chatbot raises which named human-behaviour issue?
options: Chatbot transcripts must be retained for seven years under the Privacy Act
Users need to know they are speaking to a machine, and to have a clear route to a human
Conversational data cannot be anonymised, because free text is inherently identifying
Users interact more slowly with a chatbot than with a conventional search interface
questions.explanation: This is the psychological response dot point — trust, transparency and explainability shape design decisions. (A) and (C) are invented compliance claims that sound authoritative.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: The top node of a decision tree, representing the entire dataset before any split, is the:
options: Root node
Internal node
Leaf node
Parent node
questions.explanation: Root node — (D) is the trap: the root is a parent node, but so is every internal node — "parent" describes a relationship, not a position. Internal nodes are decision points on features, branches are paths, and leaf nodes hold the final classification or prediction.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: Pruning a decision tree means:
options: Reordering the features so the most informative split is made first
Adding sub-nodes so the tree captures more of the training data
Removing sub-nodes in order to reduce overfitting
Removing training records that the tree consistently misclassifies
questions.explanation: (D) is a tempting misreading — pruning cuts the model, not the data. Over-aggressive pruning causes the opposite failure, underfitting, where the tree is too simple to capture the real pattern.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: The Gini index measures:
options: The purity of a node — the extent to which it contains a single class
The randomness or disorder present within a node
The improvement in purity produced by making a particular split
The depth at which a node sits within the tree
questions.explanation: Purity — A pure node contains only one type of outcome. (B) is entropy and (C) is information gain — all three are quantities computed at the same moment when choosing a split, which is precisely why they are so easily confused.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: A traditional decision tree differs from an ML decision tree because the traditional one is:
options: Restricted to binary splits, whereas an ML tree may branch many ways at once
Trained on historical data and updated whenever it is retrained
A static, rule-based structure defined by domain experts, which does not adapt to new data
Built upward from the leaves, whereas an ML tree is built downward from the root
questions.explanation: (B) describes the ML tree — the two halves of the comparison swapped. (A) and (D) are invented technical-sounding claims. ML trees learn patterns from data, adapt on retraining, and model non-linear relationships; this comparison is a ready-made "compare and contrast" answer.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: Decision trees can be used for:
options: Regression only, since the splits are made on numeric thresholds
Classification only, since the leaves hold discrete class labels
Both classification and regression
Clustering, since each leaf defines a group of similar records
questions.explanation: Both — a regression tree's leaves hold a numeric value rather than a class. (D) is the interesting distractor: a tree does end up partitioning the data into groups, but it does so using labels, which makes it supervised rather than clustering. Their standout advantage is interpretability — every path reads as an IF-THEN rule.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: In a neural network's input layer, each neuron represents:
options: One output class the network is able to predict
One record in the training dataset
One weight connecting to the first hidden layer
One feature of the input data
questions.explanation: One feature — (B) is the common confusion — records are fed through the network one at a time (or in batches), they are not each given a neuron. (A) describes the output layer, where each neuron gives a probability and the highest is chosen.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: A neuron computes its output by:
options: Applying an activation function to each input, then summing the results and adding a bias
Summing each input multiplied by its weight, adding a bias, then applying an activation function
Summing the inputs, applying an activation function, then multiplying by the weights
Averaging the weighted inputs, then subtracting the bias
questions.explanation: Every option contains the same ingredients in a different order, so the sequence is the whole question. Each node is effectively its own linear regression model — inputs, weights, a bias, an output — with a non-linearity applied at the end.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: Inputs x₁ = 0.8 and x₂ = 0.3, with weights w₁ = 0.5 and w₂ = 0.9 and a bias of 0.1, produce a weighted sum of:
questions.explanation: 0.77 — (0.8 × 0.5) + (0.3 × 0.9) + 0.1 = 0.4 + 0.27 + 0.1 = 0.77, which is then passed through the activation function. Each wrong option is a specific slip: (A) omits the bias, (C) pairs each input with the wrong weight, (D) adds the inputs without weighting them at all.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: The bias in a neuron is equivalent to which part of y = mx + b?
options: The slope, m
The y-intercept, b
The input variable, x
The predicted output, y
questions.explanation: The y-intercept — The weight corresponds to the slope, m — which is what makes (A) the trap. Both bias and weight are parameters learned during training, unlike x and y, which are data.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: An activation function exists to:
options: Decide how many neurons the next layer will contain
Adjust the neuron's weights in the direction that reduces the network's error
Measure how far the network's output is from the correct answer
Determine whether and how strongly a neuron fires, mapping the weighted sum into a bounded range
questions.explanation: It is commonly a sigmoid, producing an S-shaped output between 0 and 1 — the same function used in logistic regression. (A) is nonsense, but (B) and (C) are not: they are gradient descent and the cost function, the two other named pieces of the training loop.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: Gradient descent is the process by which a model:
options: Scales the input features so that no single feature dominates the weighted sum
Measures the error between the network's prediction and the correct label
Adjusts its weights and biases in the direction that reduces error, minimising the cost function
Reduces the number of hidden layers until the network stops overfitting
questions.explanation: (B) is the cost function itself — the thing gradient descent minimises, not the minimising. The two are named in the same sentence in almost every explanation, which is exactly why they get swapped under exam pressure.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: A CNN is typically used for:
options: Sales forecasting from a time series
Image recognition
Clustering customers by purchasing behaviour
Rule-based approval decisions
questions.explanation: Image recognition — (A) is the sharpest trap — that is an RNN, identified by its feedback loops, which is the architecture for sequential prediction.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: Deep learning refers to:
options: Any system that uses a neural network, regardless of the network's size
Neural networks with many hidden layers, combining inputs in progressively more complex ways
Training on a very large dataset, regardless of which model is used
Training a model over a very large number of epochs until the error stops falling
questions.explanation: The "deep" refers to layers, not to data volume (C) or training duration (D). The costs are computational expense and reduced interpretability — the deeper the network, the harder it becomes to explain any individual decision.

questions.topic: Models — decision trees and neural networks
questions.stem: A hidden layer in a neural network:
options: Holds the training labels used to correct the network's predictions
Performs computations and transformations between the input and output layers
Stores the learned weights so they can be reused between training runs
Produces the network's final prediction as a probability per class
questions.explanation: (D) is the output layer. More hidden layers means a deeper network capable of representing more complex relationships — and a less explainable one.

questions.stem: In y' = b + w₁x₁, w₁ represents:
options: The feature value supplied as the input
The bias — the value of y' when the feature is zero
The weight — the feature's importance, equivalent to the slope
The predicted label the model outputs
questions.explanation: Weight — y' is the predicted label, b is the bias (y-intercept), x₁ is the feature. Multiple features extend it: y' = b + w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + w₃x₃ …

questions.stem: Logistic regression is used for:
options: Binary classification — the output is one of two classes
Predicting a continuous numeric value from one or more features
Grouping unlabelled records into a chosen number of clusters
Reducing the number of features while preserving most of the variance
questions.explanation: Despite its name it is a classification algorithm — a classic multiple-choice trap, and (B) exists solely to catch anyone who answered from the word "regression". It applies a sigmoid to output a probability between 0 and 1, thresholded at typically 0.5.

questions.stem: Which threshold value is normally used with logistic regression?
questions.explanation: 0.5 — A probability at or above the threshold is assigned to class 1. The threshold can be tuned — lowered to catch more positives when a false negative is costly, as in disease screening — which is worth naming for an extra mark.

questions.stem: Predicting house prices from size and location is best served by:
options: Linear regression
Logistic regression
K-Means clustering
KNN classification
questions.explanation: Linear regression — the output is a continuous numeric value. (B) would only tell you which of two classes the house falls into. XGBoost is also named for regression problems.

questions.stem: KNN classifies a new data point by:
options: Splitting on the feature that produces the greatest reduction in Gini index
Assigning it to whichever of k cluster centroids it lies nearest to
Taking the majority class of the k closest existing points
Passing the weighted sum of its features through a sigmoid function
questions.explanation: (B) is K-Means — the near-miss this question exists for. Its assumption is that similar points sit near each other, which is why feature scaling and the choice of distance metric matter so much.

questions.stem: KNN's two hyperparameters are:
options: The value of K and the number of clusters to form
The learning rate and the number of epochs
The weights and the bias
The distance metric and the value of K
questions.explanation: (A) is the trap: KNN has no clusters to form. (C) are parameters learned by a model rather than hyperparameters chosen by the developer — and KNN learns neither, since it stores the data instead.

questions.stem: K in KNN should generally be an odd number because:
options: It avoids ties in the majority vote
It reduces the memory required to hold the training set
An even K makes the algorithm more prone to overfitting
It guarantees that every class is represented among the neighbours
questions.explanation: With K = 4 and a two-class problem, a 2–2 split has no winner. Separately: data with more outliers benefits from a larger K, which smooths the decision boundary, while a very low K overfits.

questions.stem: KNN is called a lazy algorithm because it:
options: Updates its model only when new labelled data becomes available
Converges on a solution more slowly than comparable algorithms
Requires no hyperparameters to be set before training begins
Stores all the training data and defers computation until a prediction is requested
questions.explanation: "Lazy" is about when the work happens, not how slow it is — there is effectively no training phase at all. The consequences are high memory use and slow prediction, so it does not scale well.

questions.stem: The curse of dimensionality describes KNN's weakness with:
options: High-dimensional input data, where points become nearly equidistant
Very small training datasets, where each neighbour carries too much influence
Datasets with many classes, where the majority vote is rarely decisive
Highly imbalanced classes, where one class dominates every vote
questions.explanation: All four describe genuine KNN weaknesses, which is what makes this hard — but only (A) is the named one. As dimensions increase, the distance between the nearest and furthest points converges, and "nearest neighbour" stops carrying meaning.

questions.stem: Which is the correct pairing of problem type and common algorithm?
options: Classification → K-Means and DBSCAN
Clustering → linear regression and XGBoost
Recommendation → SVD and KNN
Regression → DBSCAN and K-Means
questions.explanation: Classification → decision trees, random forest, neural networks. Regression → linear regression, XGBoost. Clustering → K-Means, DBSCAN. Deep learning → neural networks, Transformers (BERT, GPT). Note KNN appears under both classification and recommendation, which is legitimate.

questions.stem: KNN and K-Means differ because:
options: KNN is supervised classification using labelled neighbours; K-Means is unsupervised clustering finding groups in unlabelled data
KNN is unsupervised clustering; K-Means is supervised classification using labelled centroids
Both are unsupervised, but KNN assigns points to existing groups while K-Means creates new ones
Both are supervised, but KNN predicts a class while K-Means predicts a continuous value
questions.explanation: A named adjacent-term trap — the shared "K" is coincidental (neighbours in one, clusters in the other), and they solve opposite kinds of problem. (C) is the most seductive wrong answer because its second half is a fair description of what each does mechanically.

questions.stem: Overfitting is best described as a model that:
options: Was trained on a dataset too small to be representative of the real population
Is too simple to capture the underlying pattern in the data
Performs poorly on both the training set and the test set
Has learned the specific detail and noise of the training set rather than generalisable patterns
questions.explanation: It scores very well on training data and poorly on unseen data. (B) and (C) are both underfitting — the opposite failure. (A) is a common cause of overfitting, not a description of it.

questions.stem: A model must be evaluated on unseen test data because:
options: A larger test set produces a more statistically reliable accuracy figure
The test set is usually cleaner, having been wrangled after the training set
Training data cannot be reused once the model's weights have been fitted to it
Evaluating on data the model has already seen hides overfitting — a model that merely memorised scores perfectly on it
questions.explanation: The labelled set is split — the model learns from the training data and is judged on the test data. (A) is a true statement about sample size that simply does not answer the question asked.

questions.stem: A hyperparameter differs from a parameter because a hyperparameter is:
options: Fixed for the life of the model and never changed after deployment
Learned by the model from the data during training
Chosen by the developer before training begins
Stored alongside the weights so that predictions can be reproduced
questions.explanation: Weights and biases are parameters learned during training; K, the distance metric and the number of hidden layers are hyperparameters set beforehand. (A) is false — hyperparameters are routinely re-tuned on retraining, which is a large part of what MLOps automates.

questions.stem: In an OOP implementation of a neural network, a Layer class would most sensibly:
options: Hold a list of Neuron objects and pass their combined output to the next layer
Hold a single weight value together with the bias that accompanies it
Store the training dataset so that every neuron can read from it directly
Implement gradient descent for the network as a whole
questions.explanation: The output of one layer becomes the input of the next — composition mirrors the network's actual structure. (B) is the granularity of a Neuron's attribute, not of a layer.

questions.stem: In Python, __init__ is:
options: The constructor, which runs automatically when an object is created
A method that must be called manually straight after an object is created
A special attribute holding the class's name and defining module
The method Python calls automatically when an object is destroyed
questions.explanation: (D) is __del__ — a real dunder method, which is what makes it plausible. self refers to the specific object the method is called on, distinguishing instance data from class-level data.

questions.stem: In OOP, a class and an object relate as:
options: An object is the blueprint; a class is a specific instance created from it
A class is the blueprint; an object is a specific instance created from it
A class defines behaviour only; an object holds the data that behaviour operates on
An object is built from several classes, each supplying one of its attributes
questions.explanation: (C) is the most sophisticated wrong answer — it sounds like a reasonable separation of concerns, but a class defines both attributes and methods, and the object holds its own copy of the attribute values.

questions.stem: super().__init__() is used to:
options: Override the parent class's constructor so that it does not run
Create a separate instance of the parent class alongside the subclass instance
Call the parent class's constructor from within a subclass
Copy every attribute of the parent class into the subclass at definition time
questions.explanation: (A) is precisely backwards — omitting super().__init__() is what stops the parent's setup from running. Inheritance lets a subclass reuse and extend a parent class, shown on a class diagram by a hollow triangle arrow pointing from subclass to parent.

questions.stem: The key difference between procedural and object-oriented programming is:
options: Procedural code executes sequentially, whereas OOP code executes in parallel
OOP treats data and behaviour as separate concerns; procedural bundles them into reusable modules
Procedural code cannot be reused, whereas OOP code is reusable by definition
Procedural treats data and the procedures acting on it as separate; OOP bundles data and behaviour together in objects
questions.explanation: (B) is the distinction inverted. OOP's advantage in an ML context is that a Neuron naturally has weights and a bias and does a forward pass — the encapsulation matches the domain.

questions.stem: In the NESA locked-down Python editor, which library is available?
options: pandas
NumPy
math
scikit-learn
questions.explanation: math — Standard library only — math, random, os and datetime. No NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib, SciPy, scikit-learn, Requests, OpenCV or Tkinter, and no internet access.

questions.stem: Implementing a regression model without external libraries means you must:
options: Calculate the weighted sum and update the weights using plain arithmetic and loops
Import scikit-learn's LinearRegression and fit it to the data
Store the dataset in a database and query it once per prediction
Restrict the model to a single feature, since multiple features require matrix libraries
questions.explanation: (D) is a plausible-sounding false constraint — nested lists and loops handle multiple features perfectly well, just verbosely. Exam questions on "programming an ML model" test whether you can express the maths in code, not whether you can call a library.

questions.stem: Which Python structure is immutable?
options: set
list
dict
tuple
questions.explanation: tuple — A list is ordered and mutable, a dict holds mutable key–value pairs, and a set is unordered and mutable with unique values only. (A frozenset would be the immutable version of the last.)

questions.stem: A for loop is described as definite iteration because:
options: Its loop variable cannot be reassigned inside the body
It is guaranteed to execute its body at least once
It cannot terminate early, since its range is fixed when it starts
The number of repetitions is known before the loop begins
questions.explanation: (C) is a tempting over-extension — break will exit a for loop at any point; "definite" describes what is known going in, not what is guaranteed. A while loop is indefinite — it repeats until a condition becomes false, however many times that takes.

questions.stem: To reassign a global variable from inside a function in Python you must:
options: Declare it again inside the function using the same name
Pass it in as a parameter and return the modified value
Use the global keyword before assigning to it
Do nothing special — assignment inside a function updates the global by default
questions.explanation: Reading a global works without the keyword; reassigning it requires global, otherwise Python silently creates a new local. (B) is a better design, but it does not modify the global — it replaces it at the call site. Heavy reliance on globals is a maintainability problem in its own right.

questions.stem: Which is a documented negative of automation for worker safety?
options: Removal of humans from hazardous tasks, reducing their exposure to injury
New human–robot collaboration hazards, as in the Tesla case study — malfunctioning machines, injuries and insufficient emergency stop mechanisms
Higher productivity per worker and reduced consumption of raw materials
More consistent product quality, which reduces the volume of rework required
questions.explanation: Tesla is the ready-made counterexample to "automation improves workplace safety" — overly complex automation caused delays, breakdowns and injuries. The other three are genuine benefits, so read the word negative in the stem.

questions.stem: Automation's effect on employment is best characterised as:
options: Net job destruction across every sector, with no compensating creation of new roles
Repetitive roles displaced, new roles created in AI training, oversight and maintenance, and existing roles requiring upskilling
Displacement confined to manual and manufacturing work, leaving knowledge work unaffected
No measurable net change, since displaced workers move into the roles automation creates
questions.explanation: (D) is the most seductive wrong answer because it sounds balanced — but the transition is neither automatic nor costless, and the workers displaced are frequently not the ones who fill the new roles. Every impact dimension is two-sided: if the verb is discuss, assess or evaluate, both sides are required.

questions.stem: According to the figures in the school notes, AI exposure across employment is approximately:
options: 40% globally · 26% in advanced economies · 60% in low-income countries
60% globally · 40% in advanced economies · 26% in low-income countries
40% globally · 60% in advanced economies · 26% in low-income countries
25% globally · 40% in advanced economies · 10% in low-income countries
questions.explanation: The direction matters as much as the numbers: exposure is highest in advanced economies, because that is where the exposed white-collar roles are concentrated — which is what makes (A) a trap. Emerging markets sit at about 40%. Roughly half the exposed roles may benefit from AI integration; the other half may see lower labour demand.

questions.stem: The environmental case against large-scale automation centres on:
options: Noise pollution from automated production lines running continuously
Physical waste from decommissioned robotic equipment and its rare-earth components
Significant energy and water consumption from training large models and running data centres
Land consumed by the expansion of automated warehousing facilities
questions.explanation: All four are arguable environmental costs, but only (C) is the one the syllabus material foregrounds — and it is the one that scales with the models, not with the buildings. Balance it against efficiency gains and reduced material waste, then make a judgement.

questions.stem: The equity concern about automation and the economy is that:
options: Automation reduces total economic productivity in the sectors that adopt it
Benefits may concentrate among the owners of automated systems rather than reaching displaced workers
Automation raises wages universally, which in turn drives consumer price inflation
The economic effects of automation cannot be measured until long after adoption
questions.explanation: Distribution, not aggregate output, is the contested point — which is exactly what makes it an ethical question rather than a purely economic one.

questions.stem: Automation affects people with disability in which two-sided way?
options: Negatively only, since automated interfaces assume capabilities not every user has
Positively only, since automated captioning and speech-to-text expand independence
Positively through accessibility tools, but negatively where systems are not designed inclusively and end up excluding users
Neutrally, since accessibility is governed by WCAG rather than by automation decisions
questions.explanation: Automated captioning and speech-to-text expand independence; an inaccessible automated kiosk removes a service that a human at a counter previously provided. The question asks for the two-sided characterisation, which rules out (A) and (B) even though each is half true.

questions.stem: Designing an AI system for use by emergency services must account for the acute stress response, meaning:
options: Under stress, users focus more narrowly and therefore read instructions more carefully than usual
Under fight/flight/freeze conditions, systems must minimise cognitive load, give real-time feedback, adapt, and use calming language
Stress increases decision speed, so the interface should present more options to exploit it
Stress affects only how quickly a user acts, not the accuracy of the decisions they make
questions.explanation: Human behaviour under stress is a design input, not an afterthought. (A) inverts the finding — attention narrows, but comprehension degrades, which is why instructions must get shorter rather than longer.

questions.stem: Cultural protocols in AI development specifically include:
options: Ensuring training data is drawn proportionally from every cultural group in the population
Ensuring the interface is translated into the languages of every intended user group
Data sovereignty over data about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities — who controls it, who may access it, and for what purpose
Ensuring model outputs avoid language that any cultural group might find offensive
questions.explanation: (A), (B) and (D) are all legitimate considerations — internationalisation, representativeness and output filtering respectively — but none of them is what "cultural protocols" names. Data sovereignty here means data is subject to the laws and cultural governance of the place and people it came from.

questions.stem: How do belief systems influence ML development?
options: Differing values determine what users regard as acceptable automation, such as attitudes to AI in healthcare decision-making
They determine the learning rate and other hyperparameters chosen before training
They set the probability threshold at which a classifier's output becomes a decision
They have no influence, since a model learns only from the data it is given
questions.explanation: It sits alongside psychological responses, acute stress response and cultural protocols in the human-behaviour dot points. (C) is the subtle one — the threshold is a values-laden choice, but it is set by developers weighing error costs, not by the belief systems of users.

questions.stem: The four sources of bias in ML are:
options: Data, human decision, generative AI, adversarial
Data, algorithmic, sampling, deployment
Training, testing, validation, deployment
Data, algorithmic, human decision, generative AI
questions.explanation: (A) and (B) each keep two or three correct terms and substitute a plausible fourth. Data bias comes from unrepresentative training data; algorithmic bias from design and parameters; human decision bias from subjective choices in labelling and development; generative AI bias from models producing stereotyped content.

questions.stem: Algorithmic bias can arise:
options: Only in neural networks, where the internal weighting cannot be directly inspected
Only when the training data is itself unrepresentative of the population
Only after deployment, once the model meets real-world data it was not trained on
Even when the underlying data is unbiased, through how features are selected, processed and weighted
questions.explanation: This is why fixing the dataset is necessary but not sufficient — feature selection, weighting and thresholds all encode choices. (B) is the collapse of algorithmic bias into data bias, which is the most common error on this topic.

questions.stem: The four bias mitigation strategies are:
options: Data pre-processing, fairness-aware algorithms, data post-processing, auditing and transparency
Data pre-processing, feature scaling, cross-validation, auditing and transparency
Data cleaning, model pruning, threshold tuning, scheduled retraining
Detect, contain, eradicate, recover
questions.explanation: (B) keeps the first and last terms and swaps in two general ML techniques that improve accuracy rather than fairness — a good reminder that the two are different goals. Name the stage each strategy operates at: before training, during training, after inference, and continuously.

questions.stem: A recruitment screening model trained on a decade of the company's own hiring records systematically downgraded women's applications. This most directly illustrates:
options: Algorithmic bias — the feature weighting placed excessive emphasis on attributes correlated with gender
Data bias — historical records from a male-dominated industry taught the model to treat maleness as a marker of success
Human decision bias — developers made subjective choices when labelling which past candidates counted as successful
Overfitting — the model memorised individual past hiring decisions rather than learning a general pattern
questions.explanation: The tell is "trained on a decade of the company's own hiring records" — the unfairness was already present in the input, before any modelling choice was made. (A) and (C) are the sibling bias categories and would need different evidence in the stem. No explicit rule was written, which is what makes this the standard illustration of how an apparently neutral, data-driven system reproduces and amplifies existing unfairness.

questions.stem: The most significant consequence of biased ML outputs is:
options: Poor and unfair performance for underrepresented groups, which erodes trust in the system as a reliable source of information
Reduced overall accuracy, since a biased model necessarily fits the majority class less well
Increased computational cost, since biased models require more retraining cycles
Legal exposure under the Privacy Act, since a biased output is a use of data beyond its stated purpose
questions.explanation: (B) is the trap worth understanding: a biased model can post excellent aggregate accuracy precisely because it serves the majority well — which is how bias survives evaluation. The 2025 marker feedback rewarded answers that used stimulus examples to identify bias categories and then explained the broader effect on usefulness, rather than restating the stimulus.

questions.stem: Explainability features are added to automated decision systems primarily because:
options: Explainability reduces training time by limiting how many hidden layers are required
Explainable models are more accurate, since the constraint forces simpler structures that generalise better
Users' psychological responses — whether they trust or distrust automated decisions — determine whether the system is used and accepted at all
The W3C requires an explanation to accompany any automated decision shown in a web interface
questions.explanation: An accurate model nobody trusts or acts on has failed on the criterion that matters. (B) is a genuine half-truth — simpler models sometimes do generalise better — but accuracy is not why explainability is added, and deep models are usually the more accurate ones.

questions.stem: A dataset has 200 labelled examples and 12 features, and the client must be able to explain every decision to a regulator. The best model choice is:
options: KNN with K = 1
A deep neural network with several hidden layers
A random forest of 500 trees, for the accuracy gain from ensembling
A decision tree, because it is interpretable and does not require a large dataset
questions.explanation: (C) is the strongest distractor — it would likely be the most accurate option, but a 500-tree ensemble cannot be explained to a regulator, which was a stated requirement. Justify with both reasons: interpretability, and the fact that 200 examples cannot train a deep network without severe overfitting. Saying why not the alternative is where the mark sits.

questions.stem: A model achieves 99% accuracy on training data and 61% on test data. The diagnosis and remedy are:
options: An unrepresentative test split; reshuffle the data and re-split it
Underfitting; add layers or features so the model can capture the pattern
Data drift; schedule more frequent retraining on recent data
Overfitting; simplify the model, prune it, or gather more and more varied training data
questions.explanation: The gap between training and test performance is the signature of overfitting — underfitting (B) would show poor scores on both. (A) is worth ruling out honestly: a bad split can produce a gap, but a 38-point one points to the model, not the shuffle.

questions.stem: A spam filter's accuracy falls steadily over six months. The most likely cause is:
options: The curse of dimensionality, as the model's vocabulary of features expanded
Overfitting at training time, which only became visible once traffic increased
Data drift — spam tactics changed, so the deployed model no longer matches the data it now sees
Model collapse, caused by the filter retraining on its own previous classifications
questions.explanation: Steadily, over time, after deployment is the drift signature — overfitting would have shown up immediately at evaluation. (D) names a real phenomenon that would require the filter to be retraining itself, which the stem does not say. The MLOps response is drift monitoring plus scheduled retraining, with versioned data and weights so results stay reproducible.

questions.stem: An enterprise wants to automate copying invoice data between two legacy systems that expose no API. The correct technology is:
options: BPA
RPA
A CI/CD pipeline
A reinforcement learning agent
questions.explanation: RPA — It drives the existing software's interface exactly as a human would, which is its whole value proposition where integration is impossible. (A) is the near-miss: this is one repetitive task, not a multi-department process.

questions.stem: Automating employee onboarding across HR, IT and payroll is:
options: RPA
BPA
MLOps
DevOps
questions.explanation: BPA — a business process spanning multiple departments and systems, as opposed to the single repetitive task RPA handles. In practice a BPA implementation often uses RPA bots for individual steps, which is why the pair is so often confused.

questions.stem: A team deploys ML models by manually copying files to a server every few weeks. The best improvement is:
options: A larger validation set, so that fewer faulty models reach the server
A CI/CD pipeline automating the build, test and deployment of the application code
A scheduled shell script that copies the model files at a fixed time each week
An MLOps pipeline automating training, validation, deployment and monitoring, with versioned data and weights
questions.explanation: (B) is the sharpest trap: CI/CD would automate the deployment but would not version the data and weights or monitor for drift, which are the ML-specific gaps. (C) automates the wrong half — the copying was never the risk; the lack of validation and traceability was.

questions.stem: Which statement about a neural network's interpretability is most accurate?
options: Interpretability decreases as depth increases, which is a genuine limitation where decisions must be justified
Neural networks are fully interpretable, since every weight in the network can be inspected
Interpretability is determined by the training data rather than by the architecture
A network becomes interpretable simply by reducing the number of input features
questions.explanation: (B) is the subtle one — the weights are all inspectable, but inspectable is not the same as meaningful; no individual weight in a deep network corresponds to a reason a human would recognise. This is precisely why a simpler interpretable model is often the better engineering choice in regulated or high-stakes contexts.

questions.stem: Predicting whether a transaction is fraudulent (yes/no) is a:
options: Regression problem
Classification problem
Recommendation problem
Clustering problem
questions.explanation: Classification — a discrete label from a fixed set, here just two. Suitable algorithms: logistic regression, decision trees, random forest, neural networks. (Fraud is sometimes also tackled as unsupervised anomaly detection, but only when labelled fraud cases are unavailable — the "yes/no" in the stem tells you labels exist.)

questions.stem: A model that must run on a device with no internet connection favours:
options: A model that retrains continuously from the device's own usage data
KNN, since it has no training phase and can therefore begin predicting immediately
A large cloud-hosted transformer, queried whenever a connection becomes available
A small, efficient model such as a decision tree or compact network deployed on-device
questions.explanation: (B) is exactly backwards for this constraint: KNN is lazy, so it must carry the entire training set onto the device and compute distances at prediction time — the worst possible profile for constrained hardware.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest evidence that an automation project succeeded?
options: The model's test accuracy exceeds that of the model it replaced
The pipeline runs end-to-end without errors and every automated test passes
A measured improvement in the target business metric against a pre-implementation baseline, with the model's ongoing accuracy monitored
The system processes more transactions per hour than the manual process it replaced
questions.explanation: (A) and (D) are the seductive ones — each is a real measurement, but each is a proxy: a more accurate model that nobody uses, or a faster process that produces more errors downstream, has not succeeded. Define the metric and the baseline before deployment, or evaluation becomes an argument rather than a measurement.

questions.stem: A model is trained on data collected only from one metropolitan area and then deployed nationally. The predictable failure is:
options: Poor performance and unfair outcomes for populations unlike the training distribution
Data drift, because the model will meet data that differs from what it was trained on
Overfitting, because the model has memorised one region's records
Increased inference latency for users located far from the training region
questions.explanation: (B) is the trap worth being able to articulate: drift is a temporal mismatch that develops after deployment, whereas this is a sampling mismatch that existed from day one. This is dataset bias from an unrepresentative sample — mitigated by representative collection plus post-deployment auditing broken down by subgroup.

questions.stem: A team removes the "gender" field so their model "cannot be biased". The best critique is:
options: Proxy features — suburb, school, career gaps, hobbies — can reconstruct the attribute, so removing the field does not remove the bias
The model needs the gender field in order to correct for known differences between groups
Removing a feature lowers the model's dimensionality, which will cause it to underfit
Bias arises during training rather than from the inputs, so removing a feature is irrelevant
questions.explanation: This is sometimes called "fairness through unawareness", and it does not work. Fairness must be tested on outcomes across groups, not asserted from the absence of an input. Note the practical irony: you often need the protected attribute recorded in order to audit whether outcomes are fair.

questions.stem: A supervised model's labels were assigned by a single annotator applying their own judgement. The bias source is:
options: Generative AI bias
Data bias
Algorithmic bias
Human decision (cognitive) bias
questions.explanation: (B) is defensible-sounding, since the labels become part of the training data — but the syllabus categorises by origin, and here the origin is a person's subjective judgement rather than an unrepresentative sample. Mitigate with multiple annotators, measured inter-rater agreement, documented labelling guidelines and auditing.

questions.stem: In a CI/CD pipeline, automated tests run:
options: On every code submission, so defects surface within minutes of being introduced
Once per release cycle, immediately before the build is shipped
Nightly, so that a full suite can run without slowing developers down during the day
In production only, against real traffic, so that results reflect real conditions
questions.explanation: (C) describes a nightly build, a real and once-standard practice — CI's defining move is shortening that feedback loop from hours to minutes. This is the practical mechanism behind DevOps's goals of speed and feedback.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly matches an algorithm to its output type?
options: KNN → a continuous numeric value only
Linear regression → a category label chosen from a fixed set
K-Means → a labelled classification for each new data point
Logistic regression → a probability that is thresholded into one of two classes
questions.explanation: Linear regression → a continuous numeric value. K-Means → unlabelled clusters, which someone must then interpret. KNN → a class (it can be adapted to regression, but "only continuous" is wrong either way).

questions.stem: A decision tree is 40 levels deep and classifies the training data perfectly. The appropriate action is:
options: Re-split the data so that a larger share of records falls into the training set
Accept it, since perfectly classifying the training data is what training is for
Increase the depth limit further, since accuracy has not yet plateaued
Prune it — that depth and that accuracy together indicate memorised noise rather than learned pattern
questions.explanation: Perfect training accuracy is a warning sign, not an achievement — it is what a model that has memorised looks like. Prune, or set a maximum depth and a minimum samples-per-leaf, then re-evaluate on the held-out set.

questions.stem: The main reason an organisation would choose semi-supervised learning is:
options: Labelling is expensive, so a small labelled set plus a large unlabelled set captures much of the benefit at far lower cost
It consistently outperforms fully supervised learning trained on the same data
It removes the need for data wrangling, since unlabelled data requires no preparation
It produces a model that is inherently more explainable than a supervised one
questions.explanation: Labelling is often the single largest cost in an ML project. (B) overclaims — with fully labelled data of the same size, supervised learning wins; semi-supervised is a response to a budget constraint, not a free improvement.

questions.stem: A virtual personal assistant repeatedly misinterprets a user with a regional accent. This illustrates:
options: Data drift, since speech patterns shift gradually over time
An NLP challenge compounded by unrepresentative training data, producing unequal quality of service
Overfitting to the test set used during model selection
The curse of dimensionality, since a speech signal has very many features
questions.explanation: Note the answer has two parts — the technical challenge and the fairness consequence — which is what a "discuss" or "analyse" verb is asking for. Named NLP challenges are accents and dialects, privacy and security, and context understanding across a multi-turn conversation.

questions.stem: Which is the most defensible order of activity for an automation project?
options: Select the model → define the problem it will solve → collect and wrangle data → train → evaluate → deploy
Collect and wrangle data → define the problem and success metric → select and train a model → evaluate → deploy → monitor
Define the problem → select the model → collect data suited to that model → train → deploy → evaluate in production
Define the problem and success metric → collect and wrangle data → select and train a model → evaluate on unseen data → deploy → monitor and retrain
questions.explanation: All four are plausible-looking plans, and the differences are in the first two or three steps. (A) is technology-led adoption — picking a model first and hunting for a use case — which is the most common and most expensive failure pattern. (C) fails more subtly: choosing the model before seeing the data biases what data gets collected.

questions.stem: Automating a decision that materially affects a person requires, at minimum:
options: Retention of the decision and its inputs for later audit under the Australian Privacy Principles
Model accuracy above an agreed threshold, verified on a held-out test set
Documented consent from each affected individual before the decision is made
Human oversight, an explanation of the decision, and a route to review or appeal
questions.explanation: (A), (B) and (C) all sound like governance requirements and two of them are good practice — but accuracy is not accountability, and an audit log helps only after the fact. This is where explainability, psychological response and ethical accountability converge, and where an interpretable model may be worth an accuracy trade.

questions.stem: In a stimulus question about bias, the highest-scoring approach is to:
options: Use specific examples from the stimulus to identify the bias categories present, then explain the broader effect on the system's usefulness and fairness
Define each of the four bias types and give a textbook example of each
Identify the bias categories present in the stimulus and recommend a mitigation strategy for each
Summarise the situation in the stimulus and then state which group is disadvantaged
questions.explanation: (C) is very close and would score well — but it stops at the fix without addressing what the bias does to the system, which is the step the 2025 marker feedback specifically asked for. Don't just restate the stimulus: explain its implications.

questions.stem: Which claim about automation is not supported by the module?
options: Automation can exclude people where systems are not designed inclusively
Automation can remove humans from dangerous tasks
Automation can concentrate economic benefit among the owners of the systems
Automation guarantees improved workplace safety in every case
questions.explanation: The word doing the work is guarantees — (B) is the same claim stated as a possibility and is well supported. The Tesla case study directly contradicts (D). Every impact dot point has a documented counterexample, which is what makes them examinable as "discuss".

questions.stem: The best justification for using a random forest rather than a single decision tree is:
options: A forest trains faster than a single tree, because its trees are built in parallel
Combining many trees reduces overfitting and usually improves accuracy, at the cost of interpretability
A forest is more interpretable, since disagreement between its trees flags the uncertain cases
A forest needs less training data, because each tree is fitted on only a subset of it
questions.explanation: (C) is the cleverest distractor — vote spread genuinely is a useful uncertainty signal, but that is not interpretability, which means being able to state the reason for a decision. The trade-off in (B) is the one running through this entire module: accuracy against explainability.

questions.stem: A model is evaluated only on the data it was trained on and reports 100% accuracy. The correct response is:
options: Reject the result — it measures memorisation, not generalisation; hold out unseen test data and re-evaluate
Accept it, but re-run on a larger training set to confirm the result is stable
Reduce the model's complexity until its training accuracy falls to a realistic level
Deploy it, and monitor accuracy against real usage after release
questions.explanation: (D) is the pragmatic-sounding trap — "we'll find out in production" means the users are the test set. Evaluating on seen data hides overfitting entirely, which is the whole reason the train/test split exists.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest concluding judgement in an 8-mark question on automation?
options: "The warehouse automated because rising order volume made manual picking the bottleneck, and because the picking zone's injury rate made it the highest-value area to change first."

"The automation raises throughput and removes workers from the hazardous picking zone, but it also displaces pickers, introduces new human–robot collaboration hazards, and concentrates the productivity gain with the owner rather than the workforce."

"Judged against efficiency gain, workplace safety and equity, the automation is justified for this warehouse — throughput rises and workers are removed from the hazardous picking zone — but the Tesla precedent shows over-automation introduces new human–robot hazards, and the productivity benefit accrues to the owner rather than the displaced pickers, so the recommendation is conditional on retraining commitments and independently audited emergency-stop coverage."
"Compared with the manual process, the automated line is faster and safer per task, but costs more to install and is harder to reconfigure when the product range changes."
questions.explanation: Criteria stated, both sides weighed with concrete evidence, and a conditional judgement made. (B) is the most dangerous near-miss: it is balanced, accurate and detailed — and it never actually decides anything, which is the difference between "discuss" and "evaluate". (A) explains and (D) compares.
